title: Intramuscular injection
what: Medicine is injected into a muscle with a syringe, usually in the buttock, thigh, or upper arm. From the muscle, it quickly gets into the blood.
why: When a medicine only comes as an injection, or needs to work faster than a tablet.
tell_doctor: If you are allergic to any medicines
If past injections caused lumps or reactions

prepare.title: Prescription
prepare.text: Injections are given only as prescribed by a doctor. If you bought the medicine yourself, bring it and check the expiry date.

prepare.title: Clothes
prepare.text: Wear comfortable clothes so the injection site is easy to reach.

bring: The medicine and syringe, if you were asked to bring your own
steps: The nurse checks the medicine and dose against the prescription
You lie on your stomach or bare your upper arm
The skin is wiped with an alcohol pad
The needle goes in quickly, and the medicine is injected slowly
The needle is removed, and the spot is pressed with a pad
feel: The needle prick: a quick, sharp pain
While the medicine goes in, you may feel pressure or burning. It depends on the medicine
Relax the muscle. It hurts less that way
after: The spot may be a little sore for a day or two
If it is your first injection of a new medicine, you are usually asked to wait 15 to 30 minutes at the clinic
Do not rub the spot hard, unless the nurse says otherwise
red_flags: Trouble breathing, a swollen face or lips, a rash all over, or weakness right after the injection: tell the staff right away or call emergency services
The injection site is red, hot, or swollen, or you have a fever

faq.q: Why is there a lump after an injection?
faq.a: Sometimes the medicine is absorbed slowly, or a tiny blood vessel is hit. If the lump hurts, gets red, or grows, show your doctor.

faq.q: Can I give myself an injection at home?
faq.a: Some injections are given at home after training. A doctor or nurse should show you how and where to inject.
